title: Vishing, smishing, and voice deepfakes
body_md:
## The channel does not authenticate the sender

**Smishing** is phishing by text; **vishing** is phishing by voice. Both use the convenience of a phone at a moment when you may be distracted. A text can imitate a delivery service or bank, and a caller can claim to be an investigator, executive or family member. Sender names, caller ID, a familiar voice and even a second matching message are weak evidence when the contact began unexpectedly.

A fraudulent delivery text may contain a short link, but a short link is not required. A readable web address can also lead to a lookalike page. The decision is based on the *request*: open the carrier’s app or type its known address yourself and check whether there is actually a parcel issue. If you were expecting a parcel, that makes the message more plausible, not authenticated. Some genuine services send texts with links; this lesson teaches a safer independent route for consequential tasks, not a claim that every text link is malicious.

In a call, the attacker may move through authority (“security team”), fear (“your money is at risk”) and an immediate fix (“stay with me and move it”). A voice clone can make a family or work impersonation feel personal. The FTC warns that short clips can be used to imitate a relative. You do not need to judge whether audio is synthetic. End the incoming call and contact the person through a number you already stored, or contact another trusted person if the first cannot be reached. For a workplace transfer, use the established approval channel and a known colleague, not the email that arrived alongside the call.

A channel switch is only useful if the new route is **independent**. Calling back the displayed caller ID, a number in the text, or a number supplied by the speaker keeps you inside their story. You may also need to wait for a clean line or use another device if a suspicious call has not fully ended. If you already tapped a link but entered nothing, close it and check through the service; if you entered credentials or paid, use the service’s verified recovery channel promptly. Do not paste a real message, code or URL into this exercise.

Practice the same choice across text and voice: identify the claimed organization, then reach it yourself.

widget_config.goal: Handle an unexpected SMS or voice request by switching to a contact path chosen before the request.
widget_config.today_action: Open a delivery or banking app from your home screen and locate its help or transaction history, so you know the route before an alert arrives.
widget_config.scope: General channel-safety practice. FTC examples are US-specific; NCSC reporting routes apply in the UK. Voice cloning is possible, not assumed in every unusual call.

sources.title: UK NCSC — how to spot a scam message or call
sources.scope: UK public guidance, published 2021, reviewed 2022; cues and independent contact, not a diagnostic test.

sources.scope: US USPS example (April 2025); verify delivery independently rather than use inbound links.

blocks.title: Synthetic: parcel text during a real delivery
blocks.situation: You expect a parcel. A text says an address field failed and asks for a small redelivery payment on a linked page. The sender name resembles the carrier.
blocks.analysis: Timing and branding make this plausible. Open the carrier app yourself or use the tracking number from your original order. If the problem exists, resolve it there. Do not use the text’s link or supply payment details solely because the charge is small.

blocks.title: Synthetic: genuine appointment reminder
blocks.situation: A clinic you use sends a reminder containing only an appointment time and says you can change it in the existing patient portal. Your portal, opened from a saved bookmark, shows the same appointment.
blocks.analysis: This may be a legitimate text. Matching information in the independently opened portal supports it. You can keep or change the appointment through that portal; there is no need to reply with medical or payment data to the text.

blocks.title: Two channels, one claim
blocks.setup: You work at a fictional community center. The first two decisions concern one text-and-call payment attempt. The third is a separate new invoice snapshot; choices from the first attempt do not carry into it. All names and accounts are invented.

steps.prompt: The text contains a supplier link and says the invoice expires at noon. What first?

choices.text: Open the center’s known purchasing system and look for the invoice.
choices.consequence: You check whether the claim exists outside the message.
choices.explanation: A real deadline can be handled through the usual records.

choices.text: Open the link because the center has a supplier.
choices.consequence: The existence of a supplier does not verify this invoice or destination.
choices.explanation: Use an invoice or system you independently access.

steps.prompt: The caller sounds like your manager and repeats the exact invoice amount. What next?

choices.text: Approve payment; two channels now agree.
choices.consequence: Both channels could be controlled or informed by the same attacker.
choices.explanation: Matching details and familiar audio are not independent approval.

choices.text: Use the center’s established approval process and message the manager’s saved work account.
choices.consequence: You seek a separate identity and payment check.
choices.explanation: If the manager is genuine, the established process still applies.

steps.prompt: Separate new invoice: you independently open the center’s purchasing system. A message in your manager’s saved work account confirms that the supplier is real, but says its bank details changed; an inbound text supplies the purported new details. No payment has been approved in this new snapshot. What now?

choices.text: Pause payment and ask purchasing to verify the new destination with the supplier through its existing contact.
choices.consequence: The changed destination receives its own check.
choices.explanation: A real supplier can confirm through a previously held contact; until then, do not pay.

choices.text: Compare the new details with the caller’s text and pay if they match.
choices.consequence: Two copies of attacker-supplied details do not authenticate a change.
choices.explanation: A recipient change needs independent supplier verification under workplace policy.

blocks.debrief: Debrief: a text and familiar-sounding call can support the same false request. The final, separate invoice tests a changed recipient even after a manager confirms the supplier exists. If you approved the earlier payment, seek the center’s verified response route promptly; replay to practise checking before approval.

questions.prompt: A text from a familiar sender name includes a readable carrier domain. What is safest for a payment request?

choices.text: Open the carrier app or site from a route you already use.
choices.explanation: Correct: a plausible display name or address does not verify the request.

choices.text: Pay through the link because it is not shortened.
choices.explanation: Long addresses can also be misleading or copied.

questions.prompt: A relative’s voice asks for urgent help, but their saved number does not answer. Best next step?

choices.text: Send the money because the voice is unmistakable.
choices.explanation: Familiarity does not establish the caller’s identity.

choices.text: Contact another trusted relative or known route before sending anything.
choices.explanation: Correct: an independent person can help check a real emergency.

questions.prompt: A real clinic reminder matches the appointment in your independently opened portal. What follows?

choices.text: Use the portal for any change; the text need not be treated as fraud.
choices.explanation: Correct: independent confirmation can validate an ordinary reminder.

choices.text: The reminder must be malicious because it arrived by SMS.
choices.explanation: The channel alone cannot classify it.
